transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in. Can you tell me what’s been going on that brought you here today?

Well, thank you for seeing me. I suppose what brought me in is... well, I find myself checking the same boxes, my daily lists, the drawers around the condo over and over again before I can move on to whatever I'm supposed to be doing. And the funny thing is, I know perfectly well I already looked. It drives my wife crazy, she's always waiting by the door for me to just leave it be. 

We actually moved into this condo a few years back. Downsized from a big place over in Oak Ridge. You wouldn't believe the amount of junk a person accumulates in forty years. I found this one box of old tax returns from the nineties recently, and I used to do all my own accounting—I got my bachelor's in engineering way back when, so I've always been pretty good with numbers. The tax code was completely different back then, let me tell you. They let you write off the strangest things. 

But anyway, where was I? Oh, right. I'll just be standing there, opening and closing the same drawer in the hallway, checking the same list, and my wife is just sighing with her coat on, waiting for me to stop looking so we can finally go to the grocery store.
When you find yourself checking the drawers or lists repeatedly, what happens if you try to stop or if something interrupts you? Do you feel anxious or upset?

Well, if I try to stop... yes, I do get a bit anxious, I suppose. It's just that I keep getting these nagging thoughts that I might have thrown away something important. You know, from my old teaching files—I used to teach a few engineering courses at the community college after I retired from the firm. Or I'll think I put a needed tool in the wrong box when we moved. I had a whole workshop in the garage at the Oak Ridge house. Built all the birdhouses for the backyard myself. Cedar, mostly. They hold up better in the rain. 

But anyway, even when I tell myself it's highly unlikely I threw out anything important, the thought just comes right back. It just sits there in my head and makes it awfully hard to settle down and enjoy the evening. We usually watch Jeopardy after dinner, but lately I can't even focus on the questions because I'm thinking about whether my good socket wrench is in the hall closet or if I accidentally put it in the donation bin. Alex Trebek, now there was a host. The new fellow is alright, but it's not the same.
Do you find that these thoughts about losing something important come into your mind even when you don't want them to, and do they bother you even when you try not to think about them?

Well, yes, exactly like I was just saying. They just barge right in. I certainly don't want to be worrying about my old teaching files. I try to push it out of my mind, tell myself it's completely unlikely I threw out anything I'd ever need again, but the thought just pops right back up and makes it impossible to just sit and relax. 

It's the same with the tools. I'll try not to think about whether I put my good micrometer in the wrong box, but the worry just sticks there. I bought that micrometer back in '72, actually, when I was rebuilding the carburetor on my Chevy Nova. Beautiful car. Mint green with a white hardtop. You just don't see cars in those colors anymore, do you? Everything on the road today is silver or black or white. They all look like kitchen appliances, if you ask me. My neighbor, Bob, he has a silver sedan and I swear he loses it in the supermarket parking lot every single week. I always tell him he should tie a balloon to the antenna... 

But anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right. Yes, the thoughts just come on their own, completely uninvited, and they bother me to no end even when I'm trying my hardest to ignore them.
When these unwanted thoughts come up, do you feel like you have to do something specific—like checking a drawer or going through a mental routine—to ease the anxiety they cause?

Yes, that's exactly it. When I get those thoughts about throwing away my old files or losing my tools, I feel like I absolutely have to go check. Like I mentioned before, I'll be standing there in the hallway, checking the same boxes, going over my lists, opening and closing the drawers in the condo over and over again. I just can't seem to move on until I do it. 

Even though I know perfectly well I already looked, I just have to look again to settle my nerves. And poor Martha, my wife, she'll just be standing by the door with her coat on, sighing and waiting for me to just leave it be. She got this lovely wool coat last winter from a boutique downtown. Navy blue with these big, beautiful brass buttons. It reminds me of the peacoats we used to wear in the Navy. I served four years, you know, right after high school before I went to engineering school. Stationed out in San Diego. The weather out there is just perfect, not like the winters we get here. The damp just gets right into your bones nowadays. 

But, uh, yes, where was I? Right, the checking. I just have to do it to ease that nagging feeling, even though it drives Martha crazy when we're just trying to get out the door to the store.
